h: Cricket, Colour and the Hundred Acre Wood
p: Here's a fact that surprises plenty of visitors: Sheffield Park has a proud place in cricket history. The 3rd Earl of Sheffield was cricket mad and staged matches here in the nineteenth century, including games against touring Australian sides, played right here on the estate's own pitch. The Earl later backed cricket in Australia so generously that the Sheffield Shield, still one of the country's major domestic competitions, is named after him. The historic ground in the parkland has been brought back into use, so keep an eye out for it.

For the garden itself, the autumn colours are the headline, with acers, tupelos and other trees turning the lakes into a painter's palette. It does get busy at the peak, so arrive as early as you can for calmer paths and the best light for photos. Spring brings rhododendrons and azaleas in big blousy swathes, and quieter months have their own charm.

Allow two to three hours for a good loop of the garden, longer if you're heading out into the wider parkland. The paths are mostly gentle, but there are some slopes and grass sections, so sturdy shoes are wise.

Afterwards, Ashdown Forest is just to the north, with heathland views for miles. This is Winnie-the-Pooh country, and you can play Poohsticks at the famous bridge near Hartfield, which younger kids absolutely love. Lewes is a short drive south too, with its castle and independent shops to round off the day.
